recommendations: Test the challenger policy. Send a random 10% of transactions and 10% of the review capacity to the challenger. Run the test for about 16 days (Step 7c). Stop the test if a kill criterion applies.

Confirm two values before the test. Finance and Marketing confirm the cost of a false decline (as-02) and the guardrail limit of 3% (as-08). These values decide the size of the decline tier (Step 7b).
Retrain the score each month on all months with labels. A monthly retrain lifts the mean PR-AUC from 0.487 to 0.576 (Part 2).
Check the PR-AUC of each month, not only the PSI. The PSI of the score stays at 0.008, but the score loses 15% of its PR-AUC (Step 6c).
Do not change the team size before the test. The lowest sum of the total cost and the team cost is at 4 analysts. It is only $1,534 each month below the current team (Step 7a).
answer: The challenger policy gives a lower total cost than the champion. It uses a GBM fraud score and the expected cost in dollars, with the same review capacity. On the test months, it decreases the total cost by $126,820 each month (42%) against our base champion.

Against the strongest champion of the ladder, the decrease is $64,274 each month. The champion is our assumption, so the lower value is the result that we can defend. The decrease is at least $53,544 each month for each cost assumption that we tested. It stops 71.2% of the fraud dollars, against 38.4% for the champion.

The price is more declines of good customers: 2.46% against 0.28%. This rate is inside the guardrail of 3% (as-08). The challenger passes 4 of the 5 branches of the evaluation framework. The branches that fail are: explainability.
